===Etymology===
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:governement|tree=+}}
From {{inh|en|enm|governement}}, from {{der|en|fro|governement}} (modern French {{m|fr|gouvernement}}), from {{m|fro|governer}} (see {{m|en|govern}}) + {{m|fro|-ment}}. Morphologically {{suffix|en|govern|ment}}. Displaced native {{noncog|ang|gerec}}, {{m|ang|leodweard}}, {{m|ang|ræden}}, {{m|ang|rǣding}} and {{m|ang|ealdordōm}}.

====Usage notes====
* In the United States, "government" is considered to be divided into three branches: the legislature (the House of Representatives and the Senate) which makes law, the administration (under the President) which runs sections of government within the law, and the courts, which adjudicate on matters of the law. This is a much wider meaning of "government" than exists in the United Kingdom where {{m|en|governance}} and other words describe the process or power of governing generally and the term "government" is used more particularly for the ruling political force of the prime minister and their cabinet ministers (what Americans would call the ''[[administration]]''). In Britain, the administrative organs of the nation are collectively referred to as "the [[state]]". In Canada ''government'' is used in both senses and neither ''state'' nor ''administration'' is used. Applied to many countries in continental Europe (when using English), the British usage is common.
* In Britain, the word is often capitalised when referring to the particular UK government. British and older works in general may distinguish between ''Government'' as the ruling body and ''government'' as the practice of governing.
